**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**

None of the eight checklist lines gets a `no`. The checklist has no line for the two problems below. Both are about the words and the job of the page, and the director should decide where they belong.

1. **Off-checklist: each card's price can be read two ways.** This is in the three price lines ($9, $29 and $79 "/ month", at about x 190–990, y 385–425) and the feature lists below them (y 455–535).
   - The subhead says "for teams of every size", yet "/ month" doesn't say whether the price is per team or per user. A buyer choosing Team at $29 could be expecting to pay $29 in total or $29 per seat. Whichever reading is wrong comes out at checkout or on the first invoice.
   - The feature lists don't say whether higher plans include the lower ones. Team lists "Shared availability, Reports" but not "Booking page" or "Email reminders". Read literally, it looks like you lose the booking page by upgrading.
   - "Calendar" isn't defined: is it one per person, or one per resource?
   - Why it matters: prices and what you get for them are the lines a viewer later holds the company to (common sense, from the copy rules in critic.md).
   - Fix: write "per month, for the whole team" or "per user / month", whichever is true. Start the higher plans' lists with "Everything in Solo, plus:" / "Everything in Team, plus:". Say what a calendar is, for example "1 person's calendar".
   - Defect. Weight: major.

2. **Off-checklist: the cards have no next step, so the page doesn't finish its job.** The three cards (y 306–570) end at their feature lists. The only action on screen is "Start free" in the header (x 1107–1216, y 14–57), and it isn't tied to any plan.
   - What the viewer experiences: they compare plans, pick one, then have nowhere to click on the card they picked. They have to go up to a generic button and guess whether it starts the plan they chose. It also isn't clear whether "Start free" means a trial or a free tier, since no plan here is free.
   - The bottom third of the screen (y 570–800) is empty, so there's room for a per-card action or a line about the trial.
   - Fix: give each card its own action that names the plan and what happens, such as "Start 14-day Team trial" (only if that's the real offer). This overlaps with the Interface and Hierarchy sections.
   - Defect. Weight: major.

3. **Off-checklist: the heading and subhead could be on anyone's page.**
   - "Pricing" (y 135–185) repeats the active nav item.
   - "Simple plans for teams of every size. Change or cancel whenever you like." (y 210–260) is stock SaaS copy.
   - Nowhere on the screen does it say what Tidewell does. A viewer has to work out "scheduling / booking tool" from the feature bullets, and nothing says why to pick it over the tool they already use.
   - Fix: make the subhead say what you get in the viewer's own terms, for example "Let clients book time with your team without the email back-and-forth". Keep "cancel anytime" as the reassurance.
   - Taste. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- **One coherent system.** One blue, one sans-serif family, one card style, one neutral grey palette. Nothing looks borrowed from another kit, so the page reads as one calm, trustworthy whole, which suits a billing page.
- **Consistent cards.** All three use the same structure (name, price, three bullets) at the same positions. The eye can scan straight across them, which is exactly what a price comparison needs.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether a free trial exists and what "Start free" leads to. This decides how finding 2 should be fixed.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** What matters first: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does one element stand clearly above the rest, by size or by contrast, so the eye knows where to start?** The "Pricing" title (x≈565–715, y≈140–185) is the largest thing on the page, but only just. Its capitals look about 36 px tall, and the digits of the three prices "$9", "$29" and "$79" (y≈385–425) look about 33 px tall, in the same bold weight and the same near-black. That makes four heavy elements of almost the same strength. The eye starts on a word that tells the viewer nothing new, since the nav already shows "Pricing" as the current page. It then drops to three prices of exactly equal weight in three identical cards, with no plan set forward as the one to pick. On a page whose job is to get a visitor to choose a plan, the viewer has to compare all three with no guidance. Source: Tschichold, *The New Typography*, and Hofmann, *Graphic Design Manual*, as given in "One element dominates" and "Contrast of scale gives the page tension". Fix direction: make one element clearly the first thing seen and set the rest back by size. Here that means shrinking the page title well below the prices so it acts as a label, and giving one plan (probably Team, as the middle option) more weight than the other two, for example a stronger border or fill, a label, or more size. Defect. Weight: major.
2. **Below the first element, can you tell each level of the text (title, headings, body, captions) from the next at a glance, with no two sizes almost the same?** The title and price numerals are almost the same size (see 1). Below them, sizes also cluster:
   - The plan names "Solo / Team / Business" (~20 px semibold, y≈350) are close in size to the subtitle (~18 px regular, y≈221). Weight keeps those two apart.
   - The feature lines (~15 px, y≈465–525), "/ month" (~16 px) and the nav labels (~16 px) look a pixel or so apart. They read as one level that was set at slightly different sizes, not as separate levels.

   The viewer won't misread anything, but the page shows sizes picked one at a time rather than from a scale. Source: Bringhurst, *The Elements of Typographic Style*, 3.1.1 "Don't compose without a scale"; Dair, *Design with Type*, ch. 8, as given in "Weak contrast is worse than none". Fix direction: limit the type to a few sizes with big steps between them:
   - one display size for the prices
   - one heading size for the title and plan names
   - one body size for the subtitle
   - one small size for features, units and nav

   Use colour or weight for finer differences. Convention. Weight: minor.

**What's working.**
- Inside each card, the order is clear. The plan name (semibold, ~20 px) comes first, then the price (bold, ~40 px), then the features (regular, ~15 px, grey). The jumps in size, weight and colour between them are obvious at a glance, so each card reads in the right order.
- "/ month" is set small, light and grey beside the numeral. The price reads first and its unit second, without competing.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 1 yes, 2 no (one element stands clearly above the rest; distinct text levels with no near-equal sizes)

I couldn't do the rest of the crit or run checks on a live page; this covers arrangement only. The layout is tidy. The main problem is that the eye path ends at the bottom of the cards with nothing to do next.

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **The arrangement doesn't lead the eye from the first element through the rest; it hits a dead end.** The path goes from "Pricing" (y≈160) to the three prices (y≈405) to the feature lists, then stops at the bottom of the cards (y≈570). No card has a button or link. The only action on the page is "Start free" in the top-right corner (1107–1216, 14–57). That is about 1000 px back along the path and above everything the visitor just compared. A visitor who has picked a plan has to go back up and find it, and it doesn't say which plan it starts. Arnheim, *The Power of the Center*: the eye should reach the end, such as a call to action, without hitting dead ends or jumping back. Fix: put the next step where the comparison ends, with one action per card at the same position in each card, so the path ends at an action. Whether these should be buttons and how they look belongs to Interface and Hierarchy. **Defect. Major.**
2. **Blocks don't all take their edges from one grid; column lines don't repeat down the page.** The header container runs x=64 to 1216 (logo left edge, button right edge). The card row runs x=162 to 1118, and the first nav item starts at x=223. The body shares no column line with the header. The card edge at 162 and the nav edge at 223 are close enough to look like an almost-match rather than a choice. The viewer won't notice it, but the page feels placed by eye, not built. Müller-Brockmann, *Grid Systems in Graphic Design*, "Construction of the grid". Fix: hang the card row on the header's columns. Either line its outer edges up with the logo and button (64 and 1216), or set the header's nav or a column line to the card edges, so one set of verticals runs from top to bottom. **Convention. Minor.**

**What's working.**
- Grouping by space is right at every level. Inside each card, the plan name sits about 30 px above its price and the features are spaced about 30 px apart. The gap from subtitle to cards (about 48 px) is clearly bigger than the gap from title to subtitle (about 32 px). The gutters between cards are an even 28 px. Each card reads as one plan, and the page reads as heading block then plans.
- The three cards are built the same way. Name, price and the three feature rows sit on the same baselines in every card, so you can compare by reading straight across a row, for example $9 / $29 / $79 or "1 calendar / Up to 10 / Unlimited". On a comparison page that matters most, and it's why the centred, symmetric row works here.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** The bottom 230 px (y≈570–800) is empty, so all the content sits in the top 70% and the frame looks top-heavy and unfinished. If this is just where the browser window ends and the page continues (FAQ, footer), it's fine. If the page really ends at the cards, it's a balance problem and makes the dead end in finding 1 worse. Check by scrolling the live page.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 11 yes, 2 no (one grid governs edges and gaps; arrangement leads the eye with no dead end).

I checked the four open lines against the reference entries; here is the report.

**Section.** Text: applies. Single-screen pricing page, 1280×800, one sans family.

**Findings**
1. **Is body text large enough to read, at least as large as the menu and button text around it?** The feature lists inside the three cards (x≈191–990, y≈458–535: "1 calendar", "Shared availability", "Priority support") look about 14 px. The nav links above (y≈36: "Product", "Features"…) look about 16 px. The feature lists are the content the buyer reads to choose a plan, yet they are set smaller and quieter than the menu. That makes them the hardest text on the page to read, and the most important thing to compare. Material Design 3 sets body text at 16 and labels at 14, so here the menu is at body size and the content is at label size. Fix: bring the feature lists up to at least the nav size (about 16 px) and keep the grey; the cards have room. Convention. Weight: minor. This is a size measured by eye, so check it in the CSS.
2. **Do headings and captions break at phrase boundaries?** The subtitle under "Pricing" (centred, y≈210–260) breaks as "…Change or cancel whenever / you like." This leaves "you like." alone on line 2 and cuts the reassurance sentence in half. That sentence is the one that lowers the risk of committing. The centred two-line block looks lopsided, with one full line over a stub. Fix: break after "every size." so each sentence gets its own line, or narrow the measure so the two lines come out close in length. Taste/common sense: the entry's source is unverified for this kind of text. Weight: minor.
3. **Copy, with no checklist line: a price that can be read two ways.** "$29 / month" and "$79 / month" (y≈405) don't say whether the price is per user or flat per team. The plans are named Team and Business, and Team says "Up to 10 calendars", so a buyer can read $29 either as the price for the whole team or as $29 per person. If they assume the wrong one, they misjudge the cost by up to 10× and later feel misled. Fix: say it in the unit, e.g. "/ month, whole team" or "/ user / month". Defect. Weight: major, because this is the number the buyer acts on.

**What's working.** The price figures ($9, $29, $79 at about 40 px bold) against the small grey "/ month" use size and weight cleanly. The price is the dominant thing in each card and the unit stays legible but clearly secondary. The page also uses one family on a tight scale: heading, card title, price, subtitle and list each have a separate job, and no two sizes collide.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the subtitle break changes at other widths (reflow).

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 28 yes, 2 no (body text large enough; breaks at phrase boundaries)

**Walk (working notes).** The first thing I see is the dark "Pricing" heading. From there the eye goes to the three large prices, and then to the blue "Start free" button at the top right, which is the only saturated block on the page. It reads as a calm, generic SaaS pricing page. I'm assuming it's the pricing page for a scheduling or booking tool, aimed at teams.

Color:
- Small palette: yes. It uses white, a navy-to-gray range for text and borders, and one blue.
- Strong color kept to a small share: yes. Blue appears only in the logo, the active-tab underline and the button.
- Clear range of light and dark: yes. Near-black headings and prices sit on white, and the structure still shows in grayscale.
- Warm forward, cool back: yes. There's no warm color, and nothing needs one.
- Matching colors look the same: yes. The blue in the logo, the underline and the button reads the same.
- No vibrating edges: yes. Blue only ever sits on white or carries white text.
- Status colors used for their usual meaning: yes. Blue is used as the brand and action color, which is normal.
- Meaning not shown by color alone: yes. The active "Pricing" tab is also marked by an underline bar.
- Dark theme background: yes. It's a light theme, so this line doesn't come up.

No line was answered `no` or `unsure`, so there are no entries to open.

**Section.** Color: applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- **One accent, used only for brand and action.** The blue appears only in the "Tidewell" logo (about x 64–155, y 35), the underline under the active "Pricing" tab (x 435–488, y 69), and the "Start free" button (x 1107–1216, y 14–57). Everything else is neutral, so the button is the only saturated block and the call to action needs no extra weight to stand out. Keep it that way: any new color would compete with it.
- **Value does the structural work.** Headings and prices are near-black, plan features and the "/ month" units are mid-gray, and the card borders are pale gray. That gives three clear steps of lightness, so the hierarchy holds without hue and would survive in grayscale or for viewers with color-vision deficiency.

**Checklist.** `Color: 9 lines, 9 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure`

**Walk (working notes).** The image is 1280×800, about one screen, so I worked from the whole image. The only picture-type element is the "Tidewell" wordmark at about (64–155, 24–48). There are no photos, illustrations or icons.
- No broken image or empty placeholder: yes
- Full quality: yes (the wordmark is crisp)
- Crops intended: yes (no crops)
- Figure-ground: yes (blue wordmark on white)
- One rendering style: yes (only one asset)
- Photos consistent: yes (no photos)
- Icons share stroke: yes (no icons)
- One viewpoint and light: yes (no scene)
- Texture restrained: yes (no texture)

No line is `no` or `unsure`, so I didn't need to open any entries.

**Section.** Pictures: applies, but only barely. The only picture element is the "Tidewell" wordmark in the nav. There are no photos, illustrations or icons.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.** The wordmark at about (64–155, 24–48) is a plain bold wordmark in a single blue. It has plenty of clear space: about 64 px to the left edge and about 68 px before "Product". Because it's one flat colour with no symbol, it will still read at favicon size or in one colour. Its blue matches the "Start free" button and the active-tab underline, so the mark and the main action look like they belong together.

**Checklist.** Pictures: 12 lines, 12 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

sections.report:
**Section.** Interface: applies. The controls are the header navigation, the current-page indicator and one "Start free" button.

**Findings**
1. **Does the screen put what the user likely needs next in front of them (a prefilled default, the next action, or the information they came for) instead of making them hunt for it?**
   - **Where:** The three plan cards (about x 162–1117, y 306–569) have no button, link or "Choose plan" action at all. The only action on the page is the header "Start free" (about x 1107–1215, y 14–57), roughly 300 px above and to the right of the cards.
   - **What the viewer meets:** Someone on a pricing page has come to compare and then pick. Once they decide "Team, $29", nothing on that card lets them take it. They have to leave the cards, find the header button, and guess whether "Start free" starts Team, Solo or a trial of something. The button names no plan. With no free tier listed, "free" also leaves open how long it lasts and whether a card is needed.
   - **Why:** This is common sense; the catalog entry's source (Tognazzini) is off the approved list. The conventions point the same way: a pricing page in this style normally puts an action in each card (Jakob's law, via Nielsen Norman Group). The 230 px of empty white below the cards (y 570–800) shows there is room.
   - **Fix:** Give each card its own action at the bottom, worded with the plan or the trial ("Start Team free for 14 days" or similar). Style one tier as the recommended choice, and keep the others secondary so there is still one primary action per view.
   - **Kind and weight:** Defect, major. This is the main job of a pricing page and the screen does not support it.

**What's working.**
- The "Pricing" nav item has a 2 px blue underline in the brand blue (about y 68–70), so the reader knows where they are without reading. It uses the same blue as the button and logo, so it reads as the system's current-state colour.
- The header has exactly one filled button in a contrasting blue. All the nav items are plain text, so the primary action is unambiguous. The problem is where it sits and what it says, not its styling.

**Couldn't judge from a still.**
- Hover and focus states on the nav links and "Start free". Focus visibility matters here because the nav links have no visible edge.

**Checklist.** Interface: 33 lines, 32 yes, 1 no (next action in front of the user)
